summary: RA-MoWE runs 12 fixed probe workflows (Direct, CoT, self-consistency, decomposition, debate, etc.) on each training query, then clusters queries by the resulting score vector (k-means, six clusters). It builds one expert workflow per cluster by AFlow-style search or a guided seed-and-edit search, and trains a BGE-MLP encoder so new queries can be routed from text alone. Evaluation covers MixBench-H (600 train / 300 test from AIME, GPQA, CodeContests, LiveCodeBench) with GPT-4o-mini and Claude Haiku 4.5, plus a 300/200 SWE-bench Verified split with a fixed Agentless-lite pipeline. The authors report paired bootstrap CIs and Holm-adjusted tests. The prespecified primary contrast (text-routed bank B vs global searched workflow D) is non-significant in every regime. The only benefits that reach significance come from routing on measured test outcomes. The paper is unusually candid about these negatives.

claims.claim: Abstract: RA-MoWE improves average task score by 4.04 points over selecting among the reference workflows while using 27.7% fewer LLM calls.
claims.evidence: This is Guided-B 0.3358 vs probe-menu-B 0.2955 (§3.3, Fig. 3): exploratory and unadjusted, with CI [0.0042, 0.0773]. App. C.5: 'the arms differ in executor, prompting, decoding, and token cap; the contrast cannot isolate embedding guidance'. C.13: 'a matched full guided-versus-unguided construction experiment … not present'. The same-executor single-call CoT reaches 0.3295 at 1 call/query. The gap is 0.0063 with CI [-0.0158, 0.0289], and B.5 says this 'does not justify a break-even claim against CoT'.

claims.claim: Workflow-affinity clusters yield specialists that improve on the global searched workflow.
claims.evidence: Only with measured test affinities (A, which uses test outcomes): Haiku 0.6097 vs D 0.5381 (+0.0717, Holm p=0.0063); SWE 49/200 vs 35/200 (p=0.0052). With GPT-4o-mini, A-D = 0.0019. The deployable text-predicted B is 0.2922/0.5214/0.2000 and 'none of its prespecified contrasts against D is significant'.

claims.claim: A text encoder can predict affinity well enough to route new queries without running probes.
claims.evidence: Cluster agreement is 37.7% (GPT-4o-mini) and 12.0% (Haiku; 277/300 queries sent to one cluster). The SWE predictor picks Direct for all 200 instances. Routing realises about 0.34 against an observed per-query oracle of 0.4961.

claims.claim: Simple fixed workflows are strong alternatives (the paper's own controls).
claims.evidence: Table 1: Direct (.2872/.5694/.2000) beats the searched global workflow D (.2722/.5381/.1750) in all three regimes. A single train-selected fixed probe (self-consistency on Haiku 0.6894; tool-use with public tests on GPT-4o-mini 0.3481) beats every RA-MoWE arm on mixed tasks, including oracle A. On Haiku, searched experts score -0.1442 [-0.1931, -0.0950] below the raw probes they were seeded from (App. C.3).

patterns.note: The expert bank is a set of fixed workflows (plan, sample, select, refine flags), selected per query by cluster. Comparisons at the same executor and queries: one well-chosen fixed workflow (self-consistency on Haiku 0.6894 vs Direct 0.5694) is a clear win over a plain call. A routed bank of fixed workflows does not beat that single fixed workflow, or D, or single-call CoT (gap 0.0063, unresolved). Searched global workflow D is below Direct everywhere. So fixed structure can help, but picking among many fixed graphs per input adds nothing that is deployable.

The 'Decomposition' probe (decompose then solve) is the closest analogue to an LLM-emitted task plan, tested at the same executor against Direct (Table 6). Mixed GPT-4o-mini 0.3254 vs 0.2872 and Haiku 0.6343 vs 0.5694, though below self-consistency 0.6894. On SWE (Agentless-lite) it collapses to 0.055 vs 0.200, which the authors attribute to conflicts with localization formatting. Per-probe CIs are not given, and SWE probes are single-turn analogues, not multi-turn DAG executors.

Searched workflows: oracle-assigned cluster search beats global search on Haiku and SWE. But D (AFlow-style global search) is below Direct in all regimes, 5 of 6 guided experts kept their unedited seed, and Haiku searched experts are 14 points below their raw seed probes (App. C.3, flagged as 'not a controlled test'). Baselines are local adaptations, not full reproductions.

Query-to-workflow routing from text. The deployable router degenerates (277/300 queries to one cluster on Haiku; all-Direct on SWE) and realises about 0.34 against a 0.4961 oracle. App. C.11: a FrugalGPT cascade at high budget (0.6228) edges single Haiku (0.5994) at higher cost; MasRouter is worse on SWE.

Unusually complete cost accounting: the probe program cost $603.90 and 115,330 calls, guided construction $1.20, serving calls per query reported. Guided-B uses 2.113 calls vs 1 for CoT at a statistically tied score.
A BGE-based encoder predicts affinity vectors. Semantic BGE/Qwen3 clusters are also tested as grouping baselines; none clearly wins.
MixBench-H puzzles plus SWE-bench Verified (300/200 repository-stratified) with a fixed Agentless-lite pipeline; 1,565 of 6,000 SWE grid cells errored and were counted as unresolved.

methodology.sample: MixBench-H 600 train / 300 test (AIME, GPQA, CodeContests, LiveCodeBench); SWE-bench Verified 300/200 repository-stratified split. Three executions per arm on mixed tasks.
methodology.baselines: Direct, train-selected probe, global searched comparator D, AFlow, ADAS, ScoreFlow, FlowReasoner (outcome-assisted), semantic/random clusters; MasRouter and FrugalGPT on SWE. All search baselines are 'documented local adaptations, not published full-system reproductions' (e.g. AFlow uses the executor as optimizer with short search; ADAS uses an executor-class meta-model).
methodology.models: GPT-4o-mini (NEC endpoint and official OpenAI endpoint in different experiments), Claude Haiku 4.5; heterogeneous-model routing in App. C.11.
methodology.variance: Paired stratified bootstrap CIs; Holm-adjusted sign-flip tests for routing families; exploratory unadjusted intervals for the guided-search contrasts, which supply the abstract's headline.
methodology.ablations: Panel width (8 vs 12 probes), partition signal (affinity, BGE, Qwen3, random), operator set, encoder variants. No matched guided-vs-unguided construction run (C.13).
methodology.contamination_controls: Train/test query split and repository-stratified SWE split. No contamination analysis of public benchmark items. Several probes and FlowReasoner use test or scorer feedback on the evaluated query; these are marked in Table 1.
methodology.languages: Math/science QA; Python competitive programming; Python repositories (SWE-bench Verified).

standards.artifacts: Evidence manifests with SHA-256 hashes and per-query records are described (App. C.13) but no public code or data URL is given.
standards.preregistration: Not a human study. The paper declares a 'prespecified primary comparison' (12-probe B vs D) and reports it as null.

biases.detail: The abstract headline compares Guided-B with probe-menu-B; the authors state those arms differ in executor, prompting, decoding and token cap, so the number cannot be attributed to embedding guidance.
AFlow, ADAS and ScoreFlow are locally weakened adaptations (short search, executor-class meta-models). ADAS scores 0.2489 on Haiku vs Direct 0.5694.
The abstract reports the comparison against probe-menu routing but not against single-call CoT (tie) or the train-selected fixed probe (which beats all RA-MoWE arms on mixed tasks).
All code tasks are Python competitive programming or Python SWE-bench repositories.
200 SWE test instances; per-cluster banks built from small partitions of 600 training queries.
No public code or data link.
The authors built MixBench-H and the method, scored with their own pipeline.

coi.affiliations: Rutgers University, NEC Laboratories America, and co-authors from the OOPMAS group.
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: None. Models are OpenAI GPT-4o-mini and Anthropic Haiku 4.5.
coi.detail: No vendor self-grading. The benchmark and the method come from the same authors.

verdict_reason: Admit for its controls rather than its headline. Statistical reporting is careful (paired CIs, Holm families, a declared primary contrast reported as null), and the authors disclose that the text-routed system does not beat its comparator, that the router collapses, and that the guided-search gain cannot be attributed. Caveats: the abstract's +4.04 points / 27.7% fewer calls is an exploratory, unadjusted, multi-factor contrast. Baselines are weakened adaptations. Every significant gain uses test-outcome information. No artifacts are linked.
applicability: For the Java team's DAG question this paper points to a default of one simple fixed workflow per task type, not a bank of searched or routed workflow graphs. At the same model and queries, one fixed workflow (sample-and-select or run-public-tests) beat Direct, the searched global workflow, and the text-routed bank, and single-call CoT tied the generated bank at half the calls. Two warnings transfer. First, a decomposition-style plan that helps on reasoning puzzles collapsed on SWE-bench (0.055 vs 0.200) because its output format clashed with the repair pipeline: a generated plan must respect the downstream tool contract, which for this team means Maven/Gradle builds and cross-repo API contracts. Second, the best workflow did not transfer across regimes (rank correlation -0.45), so any workflow chosen on puzzles or on one repository must be re-measured on the team's own repositories.

conflicts_with.detail: Same author group. OOPMAS claims +18 points for per-query generated workflows on similar mixed math/code/QA streams. Here, without test-outcome access, routed or generated workflows do not beat Direct or single-call CoT significantly, which suggests OOPMAS's gain comes from its in-loop oracle feedback.

OpenCollab's code-scripted sample-two-coders-and-select workflow (Duo) beats a single agent at the same model on SWE-style tasks (DeepSWE 69.91 vs 55.75). Here the analogous fixed self-consistency probe does not help on SWE-bench Verified (0.190 vs Direct 0.200). The executors differ (multi-turn agent vs single-turn Agentless-lite), so whether sample-and-select fixed workflows pay off on code repair appears to depend on the executor.
